newsitem.title: USA: Fed statement leaves door open for more hikes.
newsitem.headline: Fed statement leaves door open for more hikes.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's statement, explaining the reasoning behind its first credit tightening in more than two years, clearly left the door open to further rate moves, economists said.

"The statement is a constructive statement. They used the term slight firming," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "There's nothing in here to suggest that they're on the war path in terms of further firming."

Platt said the factors Fed policymakers referred to in their press release were the obvious ones and ones many can agree with. There is no surprise as to what central bankers did and nothing especially surprising or distressing in their announcement, Platt added.

"The prudent investor should just play it day-to-day with the (economic) data. The prudent move is to go back to a data-dependent contingent mode here in terms of determining the next Fed move," Platt said.
The Fed said it was taking a "prudent step" in light of persistent strength in U.S. demand to extend the economic expansion.

Financial market participants had said the wording accompanying any Fed announcement would be especially important as it could signal the beginning of another cycle of tightening or merely indicate the rate hike was meant as an insurance measure to enable the current expansion to continue.

"It was a classic piece of 'Fedspeak.' It was not presented as a move designed to dampen but to sustain economic growth as the expansion goes forward," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago.
Karadakis said the statement did leave the door open for additional moves should the same set of circumstances persist down the road. But further moves were not hinted at.

When Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan reiterated the need for the Fed to be preemptive in battling inflation before Congress last week, most analysts read that as his final warning that he would tighten credit.

"I was fairly neutral in terms of what they would do. But the bottom line is if the economy's growth is sustained -- and I think it will be at least until May -- they will move again," said Jerry Zukowski, an economist at PaineWebber Inc.
The statement should not be read as a leading indicator for their next move, Zukowski said.
